```
DIR="$( cd "$( dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}" )" >/dev/null 2>&1 && pwd )"
source "$DIR/helpers.sh"
logname="make.sh"

if [ "$#" -lt 2 ]; then

PROJECT="$1"
shift

# steering options
source_config outputPath contribPath binaryTag buildPath ccachePath useCcache useDistcc cmakePrefixPath monoBuild cmakeInstallSymlinks buildJobs \

# DEBUG_CCACHE=true

export BUILD_JOBS=$buildJobs
printenv | sort > "$OUTPUT/make.sh-$BINARY_TAG.env"

# In order to maintain cache hits for out of source builds, we need to
# make sure that the relative location between the build directory and
# the sources is always the same. Otherwise, the ccache keys will contain
# unstable path components like absolute paths (because of how
# CCACHE_BASEDIR works).
#
# The naive way to achieve this would be to "symlink" the real build
# directory into its usual location under the source directory. We can't
# actually use symbolic links because cmake doe not support this, see
#     https://discourse.cmake.org/t/symlinks-on-macos-can-result-in-error-still-dirty-after-100-tries-when-using-ninja/3647
# Another option is to use bindfs
#     https://web.archive.org/web/20161124231755/http://www.redbottledesign.com/blog/mirroring-files-different-places-links-bind-mounts-and-bindfs
# but that becomes clumsy and has limits.
#
# It's much simpler to do it the other way around, link the sources into
# the build directory as suggested in
#     https://github.com/ccache/ccache/issues/751#issuecomment-756376062
#
# The somewhat nonstandard "stack" symlink is also maintained when the
# build directory is a subdirectory of the source directory (in-source builds).
# This ensures that the same cache applies for both kinds of builds.
BUILDDIR=$BUILD_PATH/$PROJECT/build.$BINARY_TAG
mkdir -p "$BUILDDIR"
ln -srTf . "$BUILDDIR/stack"
shopt -s extglob
```

```
#!/bin/bash

if [[ "$PWD" == *"/CMakeFiles/CMakeTmp" ]]; then
    # disable distcc for the calls during CMake configure
    if [[ "$COMPILER_PREFIX" == *"distcc" ]]; then
        unset COMPILER_PREFIX
    elif [[ "$CCACHE_PREFIX" == *"distcc" ]]; then
        unset CCACHE_PREFIX
    fi
fi

args=()
[ -n "$COMPILER_PREFIX" ] && args+=("$COMPILER_PREFIX")

# Since CMake 3.21 the ninja generator uses aboslute paths in the
# arguments passed to the compiler [1]. In principle we can deal
# with this by using ccache's base_dir, however, it seems that it
# handles symlinks in paths by canonicalizing them [2], which is
# not what we want in order to share the cache between in-source
# and out-of-source builds.
# Instead, we will just do the prefix removal ourselves here,
# which keeps the symlink and the paths look identical independent
# of where the build directory is.
# Note that we don't handle -isystem includes from upstream projects
# we built, since base_dir works fine for the InstallArea-s.
#
# [1] https://gitlab.kitware.com/cmake/cmake/-/merge_requests/6148
# [2] https://www.mail-archive.com/ccache@lists.samba.org/msg01385.html

if [[ "$BUILDDIR" == "$PWD" ]]; then
    for arg in "$@"; do
        arg="${arg/#-I$BUILDDIR\//-I}"  # substitute "-I$BUILDDIR/x/y.h" with "x/y.h"
        arg="${arg/#$BUILDDIR\//}"   # handle "$BUILDDIR/x/z.cpp" and "$BUILDDIR/toolchain/g++..."
        args+=($arg)
    done
else
    args+=("$@")
fi

exec "${args[@]}"
```

```
export PATH=$CONTRIB/bin:$PATH
# force a particular ninja executable since for some reason CMake does not
# look into PATH and picks up /usr/bin/ninja-build when present.
export CMAKE_MAKE_PROGRAM=$CONTRIB/bin/ninja
# more informative build progress [notstarted>running>finished/total]
export NINJA_STATUS="[%u>%r>%f/%t] "


setup_ccache() {
  export CCACHE_DIR="$ccachePath"

  # Setup ccache limits only if not setup
  [ ! -d "$CCACHE_DIR" ] && ccache -F 20000 -M 0

  # Use a fast directory for temporaries
  export CCACHE_TEMPDIR="$TMPDIR/ccache-tmp"
  # Use some sane sloppines (see ccache docs)
  # - set locale to C to get consistent compiler messages
  # - only include system headers in the hash but not add the system header files to the list of include files
  #   This allows ccache to only check non-system headers, but will also cause
  #   it to return stale cache hits if such system headers have been changed.
  export LANG=C LC_ALL=C LC_CTYPE=C LC_MESSAGES=C
  # export CCACHE_SLOPPINESS="locale,system_headers"
  export CCACHE_SLOPPINESS="locale"
  # FIXME: system headers are cannot be ignored at present because upstream
  #        projects are included as -isystem .
  #        See https://gitlab.cern.ch/lhcb/LHCb/-/issues/191
  export CCACHE_COMPILERCHECK="none"
  # Do not check the compiler as its name is always in the cache key
  # and it is already unique (e.g. "g++-11.1.0-e80bf-2.36.1-a9696"), see toolchain.cmake
  # FIXME: We can remove this once the lcg-toolchains wrapper is fixed
  #        to not depend on PATH and have the wrapper content stable.

  # Increase hit rate by
  # - rewriting absolute paths that start with $BUILD_PATH into relative ones
  #   So a compilation unit in LHCb which for example includes -I /full_path_to_lb_stack_folder/Gaudi/InstallArea/...
  #   will have its path rewritten (before ccache hashes) to one that is relative
  #   to the build directory (where the compiler runs).
  export CCACHE_BASEDIR="$BUILD_PATH"
  # - rewrite absolute paths in stderr to not get wrong paths in e.g. warning messages
  export CCACHE_ABSSTDERR=1
  # - using -ffile-prefix-map (see toolchain.cmake). CCACHE_NOHASHDIR=1 is not needed.
  #   See https://ccache.dev/manual/latest.html#_compiling_in_different_directories
  #   Needs recent distcc server, see https://github.com/distcc/distcc/pull/459

  # Secondary cache
  export CCACHE_SECONDARY_STORAGE="$ccacheHosts"

  # Use generated depenencies instead of the preprocessor, much faster!
  export CCACHE_DEPEND=1
  # Keep track of stats for this build.
```

```
// Main execution
  //=============================================================================
  Tracks HybridSeeding::operator()( const FT::Hits& hits, ZoneCache const& zoneCache, DeMagnet const& magnet ) const {
    const auto scopedTimer = m_timerTool.get()->scopedTimer( m_timerIndex, m_timerTool.isEnabled() );
    // Containers
    TrackCandidates trackCandidates; //---LoH: probably could be changed to array(static_vector)
    XCandidates     xCandidates;     //---LoH: probably could be changed to static_vector
    TracksToRecover tracksToRecover; //---LoH: probably could be changed to static_vector

    trackCandidates[0].reserve( m_nTrackCandidates );
    trackCandidates[1].reserve( m_nTrackCandidates );
    xCandidates[0].reserve( m_nXTrackCandidates );
    xCandidates[1].reserve( m_nXTrackCandidates );
    tracksToRecover[0].reserve( m_nXTrackCandidates );
    tracksToRecover[1].reserve( m_nXTrackCandidates );

    //==========================================================
    // Hits are ready to be processed
    //==========================================================
    unsigned int             nHits         = hits.size();
    PrFTHitHandler<ModPrHit> oriHitHandler = makeHitHandler( hits );
    SmallDexes               oriSmallDexes( nHits, 0 );
    updateSmallDexes( oriSmallDexes, oriHitHandler );

    PrFTHitHandler<ModPrHit> tmpHitHandler;
    SmallDexes               smallDexes = oriSmallDexes;

    PrFTHitHandler<ModPrHit>* hitHandler = &oriHitHandler;
    //========================================================
    //------------------MAIN SEQUENCE IS HERE-----------------
    //========================================================
    auto main_loop = [&]( auto icase ) {
      //----- Loop through lower and upper half
      std::array<unsigned int, nParts> nTracksBefore;
      for ( unsigned int part = 0; nParts > part; ++part ) {
        nTracksBefore[part] = trackCandidates[part].size();
        xCandidates[part].clear(); // x candidates up cleaned every Case!
        findXProjections( hits, zoneCache, part, icase, *hitHandler, xCandidates );
        if ( m_removeClonesX ) {
          if ( m_removeClones_forLead )
            removeClonesX_sorted( part, xCandidates, m_removeClones_distance, m_removeClones_sorted_distance );
          else
            removeClonesX_pp( part, xCandidates, m_removeClones_distance );
        } //---LoH: this probably should be encoded in the logic. Clone tracks are close to each other.
        m_outputXZTracksCnt_part[part] += xCandidates[part].size();
        m_outputXZTracksCnt_cases[icase] += xCandidates[part].size();
        addStereo<icase> addStereoCase( *this, tracksToRecover );
        addStereoCase( hits, zoneCache, part, *hitHandler, trackCandidates, xCandidates );
        m_outputTracksCnt_cases[icase] += trackCandidates[part].size();
      }
      // Flag found Hits at the end of each single case ( exclude the latest one )
      if ( ( icase + 1 < NCases ) ) {
        for ( unsigned int part = 0; nParts > part; ++part )
          flagHits( icase, part, trackCandidates, nTracksBefore[part], hits, smallDexes, *hitHandler );
        tmpHitHandler = consolidateHitHandler( *hitHandler );
        hitHandler    = &tmpHitHandler;
        updateSmallDexes( smallDexes, *hitHandler );
      }
    };
    Utils::unwind<0, NCases>( main_loop );

    // Recovering step
    if ( Recover ) {
      xCandidates[0].clear();
      xCandidates[1].clear();
      int totCands = -( trackCandidates[0].size() + trackCandidates[1].size() );
      RecoverTrack( hits, zoneCache, oriSmallDexes, oriHitHandler, trackCandidates, xCandidates, tracksToRecover );
      m_outputTracksCnt_cases[NCases] += ( totCands + trackCandidates[0].size() + trackCandidates[1].size() );
    }

    // Clone removal ( up/down )
    for ( unsigned int part = 0; part < nParts; ++part ) {
      if ( m_removeClones_forLead )
        removeClones_lead( part, trackCandidates, m_removeClones_distance );
      else
        removeClones_pp( part, trackCandidates, m_removeClones_distance );
      m_outputTracksCnt_part[part] += trackCandidates[part].size();
    }

    Tracks result;
    result.reserve( trackCandidates[0].size() + trackCandidates[1].size() );
    // Convert LHCb tracks
    for ( unsigned int part = 0; part < nParts; ++part ) {
      makeLHCbTracks( hits, result, part, trackCandidates, magnet );
    }
    return result;
  }
```

<sub>76m 23s</sub>

### Copilot

**What seeding is.** The SciFi tracker (T1–T3) sits *after* the magnet. Each station has 4 layers, ordered X, U, V, X. The X layers are vertical, and the U/V layers are tilted by ±5°. A "seed" is a track segment found using only SciFi hits, with no VELO or UT information. Seeds are used for downstream and T-tracks, and for long-lived particles such as Ks and Λ. In the field-free region the track is nearly a straight line in y–z. In x–z it is a parabola, because of the residual field.

**CPU version: `Rec/Pr/PrAlgorithms/src/PrHybridSeeding.cpp`.** "Hybrid" means it looks at X and stereo layers in separate steps.
1. Split the hits into two halves, `part` 0 (lower) and 1 (upper).
2. Run a number of cases (`NCases`). Each case picks a different set of X layers as first, last and middle. In each one `findXProjections` builds x–z tracks:
   - Two hits (first and last layer) define a parabola.
   - A search window in the middle layers picks up more hits.
   - Hits must fit within a tolerance, and the track needs a minimum hit count.
3. `removeClonesX` drops duplicate x–z candidates.
4. `addStereo` adds U/V hits. It uses the y–z fit to compute the y and z positions, then fits XYZ. A beam-hole filter is applied.
5. After each case it flags the hits already used and rebuilds the hit handler, so later cases see fewer hits.
6. A `Recover` step re-tries the leftover x–z candidates.
7. It runs clone removal across tracks and converts the result to LHCb tracks. Momentum comes from the x–z curvature through `makeLHCbTracks` and `DeMagnet`.

**GPU version (HLT1): `Allen/device/SciFi/hybridseeding`.** It has a similar structure. `seed_xz.cu` builds the x–z tracks from triplets (hit indices packed into 32 bits). `seed_confirmTracks.cu` then adds the stereo hits. Both are limited by per-event hit counts such as `maxNHits`. This is to meet the HLT1 throughput budget.

Which part do you want to look at in more detail?

<sub>77m 40s</sub>

### User

Is "seeding" reconstructing a trck from SciFi hits?

---

<sub>77m 44s</sub>

### Copilot

Yes. Seeding reconstructs a track from SciFi hits only. The result is a "T-track" or "seed", which is a partial track segment found after the magnet.

- **What's included:** the SciFi hits alone give a position and direction, plus a rough momentum from the curvature of the x–z parabola. That momentum is only approximate, because there is no VELO vertex to anchor it.
- **What's not included:** the part of the track before the magnet. That comes from VELO and UT, and a seed has none of it.

Seeds are then used in two ways:
- **Matching:** they can be joined to VELO tracks to form long tracks, which is the "Matching" algorithm.
- **Standalone:** they can be kept as T-tracks or extended with UT hits to form downstream tracks. These are needed for particles that decay outside the VELO, such as Ks and Λ.

---

<sub>79m 18s</sub>

### User

How to evaluate whether the seeding did a good job or not?

---

<sub>79m 24s</sub>

### Copilot

Evaluate it by matching reconstructed seeds to simulated (MC) particles and measuring a few quantities.

**1. Truth matching.** A seed is matched to an MC particle if enough of its hits come from that particle. In LHCb the usual criterion is that at least 70% of the hits belong to the same MC particle. Everything else is unmatched.

**2. Efficiency.** This is the fraction of reconstructible particles that are found.
- *Reconstructible* means the particle left enough hits in the SciFi (at least one X and one stereo hit in each of the 3 stations).
- Quote it as a function of p, pT, η, and the number of primary vertices.
- Compute it for particle categories such as "long", "from B" and "from strange", and with or without electrons.

**3. Ghost rate.** This is the fraction of reconstructed seeds that don't match any MC particle. It can be quoted per event or as a fraction of seeds, and also as a function of p, pT, η and event multiplicity.

**4. Clone rate.** This is the fraction of seeds that match a particle which another seed has already matched. Clone removal is meant to keep this low.

**5. Resolution and purity.**
- Hit purity, meaning the fraction of hits on the seed that come from the matched particle.
- Residuals and pulls of position (x, y) and slopes (tx, ty) against the MC truth at a reference z.
- Momentum resolution, `(p_reco − p_true) / p_true`. Seed momentum is worse than a full fit, so compare it against a baseline.

**6. Timing.** This is the CPU time per event for the Rec version, or throughput for the Allen version. It is especially important for HLT1.

**Tools in the stack**
- `PrChecker` (`PrTrackChecker`) computes efficiency, ghost rate and clone rate against MC. I haven't looked at how it is configured for SciFi seeds, so that needs checking.
- Allen has its own checker for its seeding output.
- For Rec you can also compare against the previous implementation of the same algorithm to catch regressions.

I can look for the checker configuration in your stack if you want.

<sub>80m 28s</sub>

### User

Input: hits; Output: an x-z parabola. right?

---

<sub>80m 32s</sub>

### Copilot

Partly right. That describes the first stage only.

**Stage 1, x–z search (`findXProjections` / `seed_xz`):**
- Input: hits in the X layers only.
- Output: an x–z parabola candidate. It has about 3 parameters (x position, slope, curvature), and the hit list comes with it.

**Stage 2, stereo (`addStereo` / `seed_confirmTracks`):**
- Input: the x–z candidates plus the U/V hits.
- Output: a full 3D seed with x(z) as a parabola and y(z) as a straight line. The y–z part is fitted from the stereo hits.

So the final seed is not just an x–z parabola. Every x–z parabola leaves y undetermined, and the stereo layers fix it. Only candidates that get enough U/V hits become seeds. The final seed also gets a momentum estimate from the curvature.

<sub>81m 19s</sub>

### User

<sub>81m 27s</sub>

### Copilot

In the Moore HLT2 reconstruction (`Moore/Hlt/RecoConf/python/RecoConf/hlt2_tracking.py`), seeds feed these steps:

1. **Matching (`PrMatchNN`)**: this makes long tracks. Each VELO track is extrapolated through the magnet and matched to a seed. A neural net (the MatchNN weights) scores the pairs, and UT hits can be added. The result is the main long-track sample.

2. **Downstream tracking (`PrDownstream`)**: for seeds that have no VELO partner, such as Ks and Λ decay products, it adds UT hits to the seed. This gives downstream tracks.

3. **Residual seeding (`PrResidualSeeding`)**: it takes the seeds that were not used in long tracks. These "residual" seeds are kept as T-tracks or passed on to downstream tracking. Their purpose is to avoid duplicate tracks.

4. **Kalman fit (`PrKalmanFilter_Seed`, `_Downstream`)**: the seeds are refitted. This gives a proper momentum and covariance.

5. **Conversion and ghost rejection.** `fromPrSeedingTracksV1Tracks` converts them to the standard track format. Ghost-probability tools then score them.

Seed quality therefore limits how well long-track matching and downstream tracking can do.

<sub>82m 53s</sub>

### User

What is a Kalman fitting or Kalman filtering? Give a simplified example, not necessarily the situation now.

---

<sub>82m 59s</sub>

### Copilot

A Kalman filter estimates a hidden quantity from noisy measurements. It processes them one at a time and updates its estimate after each. It keeps two things: the **estimate** and its **uncertainty**.

**Example: locating a car on a line**

Suppose a car moves at roughly 10 m/s and a GPS reports its position every second, with 5 m error.

Each step has two parts:

1. **Predict.** Move the estimate forward using the motion model. Uncertainty grows, because the model is imperfect.
   - Last estimate: 100 m, ±2 m. Prediction: 110 m, ±3 m.

2. **Update.** A measurement arrives: 116 m, ±5 m. Combine the two, weighting each by its precision.
   - The **Kalman gain** is `K = σ_pred² / (σ_pred² + σ_meas²) = 9 / (9 + 25) ≈ 0.26`.
   - New estimate: `110 + 0.26 × (116 − 110) ≈ 111.6 m`.
   - New uncertainty: `σ² = (1 − K) σ_pred² ≈ 6.6`, so ±2.6 m. That is better than either input alone.

The more precise source pulls the estimate harder. Repeating this over many measurements gives an estimate that is more accurate than any single one.

**In a tracker.** The "car" is the particle's state `(x, y, tx, ty, q/p)`. The "predict" step extrapolates it from one detector layer to the next. It accounts for the magnetic field and for scattering in material, which adds uncertainty. The "update" step blends in the hit on that layer. At the end you get the best estimate of position, direction and momentum, with a covariance matrix and a χ² for the fit quality.

In practice, a forward pass is usually followed by a backward smoothing pass. This gives the best estimate at every point on the track.

<sub>83m 32s</sub>

### User

Is the measurement of SciFi here a noisy measurement?

---

<sub>83m 36s</sub>

### Copilot

Yes. Each SciFi hit is a noisy measurement of where the particle crossed that layer.

**Sources of noise**
- **Finite resolution.** The fibre mats read out clusters of channels with ~250 µm pitch. The resolution on the x position is around 60–80 µm.
- **Clustering.** The position comes from the light shared among neighbouring channels, so it has an error.
- **Geometry.** Misalignment and calibration errors add a systematic offset.
- **Only x is measured well.** A single layer measures a position across the fibre direction. The position along the fibre is unknown, which is why the stereo layers are tilted by ±5°.

**Why it matters for the fit.** Each hit is given an uncertainty, which acts as the measurement error σ in the Kalman update. The fitter weights hits by it.

**A second source of "noise":** a hit can also be wrong rather than imprecise. It may belong to a different particle, or be noise or a ghost hit. The Kalman filter doesn't handle that by itself. The χ² of the fit and outlier removal do.

```
@configurable
def make_PrHybridSeeding_tracks(
    make_ft_hits=make_PrStoreSciFiHits_hits,
    clusters_on_track_tool=get_global_clusters_on_track_tool_no_ut,
    FasterCloneRemoval=False,
):
    """Makes seed tracks with PrHybridSeeding [1]_.

    Args:
        make_ft_hits (DataHandle): maker of FT hits, defaults to `make_PrStoreSciFiHits_hits <RecoConf.legacy_rec_hlt1_tracking.make_PrStoreSciFiHits_hits>`.
        clusters_on_track_tool (Callable): function to get an ITrackAddClusters tool. "NoUT" version by default, as UT hits are not needed.
        FasterCloneRemoval (bool): Switch for faster clone removal (RemoveClones_forLead). Defaults to False.

    Returns:
        A dict mapping v1 and v2 SciFi seeding tracks to ``'v1'`` and ``'v2'`` respectively.

    .. [1] https://cds.cern.ch/record/2027531/

    """
    scifi_tracks_pr = PrHybridSeeding(
        FTHitsLocation=make_ft_hits(),
        RemoveClones_forLead=FasterCloneRemoval,
    ).OutputName

    scifi_tracks_v1 = fromPrSeedingTracksV1Tracks(
        InputTracksLocation=scifi_tracks_pr,
        TrackAddClusterTool=clusters_on_track_tool(),
    ).OutputTracksLocation

    return {"v1": scifi_tracks_v1, "Pr": scifi_tracks_pr}


@configurable
def make_seeding_tracks(make_seed_tracks=make_PrHybridSeeding_tracks):
    return make_seed_tracks()
```

### Copilot

I've written the code map to `/afs/cern.ch/work/x/xihu/stack/stack/SciFi_seeding_code.md`. It lists the files by area:

- **Rec, CPU/HLT2:** `PrHybridSeeding.cpp` is the algorithm. `PrHybridSeedTrack.h`, `HoughSearch.h` and the `PrTrackFitterXZ`, `PrTrackFitterYZ` and `PrTrackFitterXYZ` headers support it. `PrResidualSeeding.cpp` handles the leftover seeds.
- **Event model and conversion:** `PrSeedTracks.h` is the output container. `fromPrTracksV1Track.cpp` converts the seeds to v1 tracks.
- **Allen, HLT1:** `seed_xz.cu` and `seed_confirmTracks.cu` do the search. The consolidate files copy the results out. The `scifi_reconstruction.py` configuration wires them together, and the host validators check them.
- **Moore configuration:** `hlt2_tracking.py`, `run5_default_tracking.py`, `hlt2_cheated_tracking.py` and `mc_checking.py`.

Two things in the document are not verified. I did not read the internals of the individual functions. I also did not check which Moore options turn seeding on for a given job.

<sub>122m 35s</sub>

### Copilot

The Kalman fit lives in `Rec/Tr/PrKalmanFilter/`. I read the outline of the code, not every function.

**Files**
- `include/PrKalmanFilter/KF.h` (1418 lines) holds the maths, in namespace `LHCb::Pr::Tracks::Fit`.
- `src/KalmanFilter.cpp` has the Gaudi algorithms, which run the fit on whole track containers.
- `src/KalmanFilterTool.cpp` has `KalmanFilterTool`, an `IPrFitterTool` for fitting single tracks. It has the properties below.
- `V1V1PrKalmanFilter.cpp` and `ToolExample.cpp` are a v1-to-v1 wrapper and an example.

**How it works in `KF.h`**
- **Nodes.** The fit runs over a list of `Node` objects. They come from `Event/PrFitNode.h`, one per hit, plus some for material and other positions.
- **`predict`.** It moves the state to the next node. The state vector is `F * previous_state + transport_vector`. The covariance is `F C Fᵀ + noise_matrix`. The noise matrix holds the multiple scattering (and energy loss through `apply_delta_E`). The backward direction does the inverse transport.
- **`filter`.** It folds in the hit with `LHCb::Math::Filter` and returns a χ² contribution. A node without a hit on the track is skipped.
- **`fit`.** It runs a forward pass from the first node. A backward pass then starts from the forward result. The two χ² values are summed, and `n_track_parameters` is subtracted from the degrees of freedom.
- **Smoothing.** `smooth_and_update_ref_vector` and its `_outlier` version build the final state at each node. They use the other direction's filtered state, and `average_node` averages the two where a hit was skipped. A classical smoother is also there (`classical_smoother_iteration_for_alignment`), and it is optional.
- **Iteration.** The fit repeats up to `MaxFitIterations` (default 10), and it updates the transport matrices and the reference states each time.
- **Outlier removal.** It looks for the worst-χ² hit above `MinChi2Outlier` (default 9) and removes it. It keeps a minimum number of hits for each detector type. It then refits, up to `max_outlier_iter` times, and checks the final χ²/ndf against `MaxChi2`.
- **Start values.** The starting state uncertainties are set by properties: `ErrorX` and `ErrorY` are 20 mm, `ErrorTx` and `ErrorTy` are 0.1, and `ErrorQoP` is 0.01.

**Track types.** The code is a template over the input type, with `if constexpr` branches for VELO (VP), UT and SciFi (FT) hits. It covers long, upstream, downstream, VELO and seed tracks. So it is the same Kalman code that refits SciFi seeds. In Moore these are `PrKalmanFilter_Seed` and `PrKalmanFilter_Downstream` in `hlt2_tracking.py`.

Two things I did not check: the extrapolators used to build the transport matrices, and the details of the material and scattering model.

```
def standalone_hlt2_seeding(do_mc_checking=False, do_data_monitoring=False):
    """Run the Hlt2 track reconstruction optimized for not having the UT detector

    Args:
        do_mc_checking (bool): Enable MC checking.
        do_data_monitoring (bool): Enable monitoring.

    Returns:
        Reconstruction: Data and control flow of Hlt2 track reconstruction.

    """

    seed_tracks = make_PrHybridSeeding_tracks()
    data = [seed_tracks["v1"]]

    if do_mc_checking:
        types_and_locations_for_checkers = {
            "Seed": seed_tracks,
        }
        data += get_track_checkers(
            types_and_locations_for_checkers,
            uthit_efficiency_types=[],
            make_links_lhcbids_mcparticles=make_links_lhcbids_mcparticles_VP_FT,
        )
        data += hits_resolution_checkers(with_UT=False)
    return Reconstruction("hlt2_reco", data, reco_prefilters())
```

<sub>969m 20s</sub>

### Copilot

**Rec (Moore HLT2), input and output**

- **Input:** raw FT cluster banks (`FTCluster` raw bank type). `FTRawBankDecoder` decodes them into `FTLiteClusters`. `PrStoreSciFiHits` then turns those into `FT::Hits`, using the mat geometry cache, and `PrHybridSeeding` reads those hits. Evidence: `make_FTRawBankDecoder_clusters` in `legacy_rec_hlt1_tracking.py`, and the `Transformer` signature in `PrStoreSciFiHits.cpp`.
- **Output:** `Seeding::Tracks`, the SoA seed container. It is written to `LHCb::TrackLocation::Seed` by default. `fromPrSeedingTracksV1Tracks` turns it into v1 tracks.
- **Also read:** the `DeMagnet` and the FT geometry from the conditions database or DD4hep.

**Allen (HLT1)** reads the same raw banks and decodes them on the device (`dev_scifi_hits`). It outputs `SciFi::Seeding::TrackXZ` for stage 1 and the consolidated seed tracks for stage 2.

**Standalone testing: yes.** The ready-made entry point is `standalone_hlt2_seeding` in `Moore/Hlt/RecoConf/python/RecoConf/standalone.py`. It runs only `make_PrHybridSeeding_tracks()`, plus the MC checkers if you ask. The example options are `Moore/Hlt/RecoConf/options/examples/hlt2_reco_seeding_with_mcchecking.py`. They call `run_reconstruction(options, standalone_hlt2_seeding)` with `do_mc_checking=True`. That runs the track checker and the hit-resolution checkers (`hits_resolution_checkers`).

**File formats.** I did not find the format settings in these options, so this part is partly my knowledge:
- **MDF:** raw data. This is the usual input for data and for Allen's standalone runs. Raw banks only, so there is no MC truth.
- **(X)DIGI / XDST:** simulation files. You need them for MC checking, because they carry the MC particles and the links to the hits. The example uses `make_links_lhcbids_mcparticles_VP_FT`, so the input needs those links.
- **The setup is usually set in an options file.** It lists the input files, the `input_type` (`ROOT` or `MDF`), the simulation flag, and the DB tags or geometry version. `Moore/Hlt/RecoConf/options/mdf_for_standalone_Allen.py` is an example of that style.

To run it you would need a built Moore, and `make Moore` failed earlier in this session. Does a Moore installation already exist on your machine, for instance under `/cvmfs`? I could check how the example options are meant to be launched.

````
### Reproduce nightly builds

Some projects might require some MRs to be applied on top
of the default branch used in the nightlies. This is reflected in the nightly
slot definitions (by using HEAD as version) and you can see the exact set of
MRs applied at the project's checkout page of a given build.

Below are two examples of how to get a checkout of Gauss that corresponds to the
`lhcb-master/1767` build (which included MRs 845 and 861).

#### Checkout and apply MRs manually

```sh
cd Gauss
git fetch && git fetch origin '+refs/merge-requests/*/head:refs/remotes/origin/mr/*'
git checkout origin/master
git merge --no-edit origin/mr/845 origin/mr/861
```

#### Checkout the nightly tags

The nightlies create a tag for each project and for each build. These tags can be used as follows

```sh
cd Gauss
git fetch ssh://git@gitlab.cern.ch:7999/lhcb-nightlies/Gauss.git lhcb-master/1767
git checkout FETCH_HEAD
```

### Update the setup

In case there is a fix or an update to the setup, just run `setup.py`

```sh
python3 utils/setup.py
```

It attempts to pull the latest `master` and to update your `config.json`.
Then, verify your configuration (to catch issues with new or modified settings).

```sh
utils/config.py
```

Finally, try to build again and follow any instructions you may get.
If that is not sufficient (e.g. because the toolchain changed),
the best is to purge all your projects with

```sh
make purge
```

### Use a non-standard branch of lb-stack-setup

You might want to use a branch other than `master` to try out a new feature
that is not merged yet.

nightly
release
scripts
test
testing
````

```
# Keep track of stats for this build.
  export CCACHE_STATSLOG="$OUTPUT/stats/$BINARY_TAG/$PROJECT.ccache-statslog"
  rm -f "$CCACHE_STATSLOG"  # clear stats

  mkdir -p "$CCACHE_TEMPDIR" $(dirname $CCACHE_STATSLOG)

    export CCACHE_DEBUG=1
    # export CCACHE_READONLY=1
    export CCACHE_DEBUGDIR="$OUTPUT/ccache-debug/$PROJECT/"
    export CCACHE_LOGFILE="$OUTPUT/ccache.log"
    rm -f "$CCACHE_LOGFILE"  # clear logfile
  fi

pump_startup() {
  # start the include server manually (instead of pump --startup) for more control
  local include_server_install=$(python -c "
import sysconfig
print(sysconfig.get_path('purelib', vars={'base': '$CONTRIB'}))
  ")/include_server
  local pid_file="$OUTPUT/distcc-pump.pid"

  # kill stray include servers (as pump relies on no changes during build)
  pkill -f "$include_server_install/include_server.py --port" || true

  if [ "$DEBUG_DISTCC" = true ]; then
    # --time = Print elapsed, user, and system time to stderr.
    # --statistics = Print information to stdout about include analysis.
    # --debug_pattern : 19 = 1 (warning) + 2 (trace 0) + 16 (data); 31 = everything
    local debug_args="--time --statistics --debug_pattern=19"
    # debug_args="$debug_args --path_observation_re=/cvmfs"
  else
    local debug_args="--debug_pattern=1"  # only warnings
  fi

  # Variable used by "pump --shutdown" (see pump_shutdown)
  export INCLUDE_SERVER_DIR=$(mktemp -d -t distcc-pump-socket-XXXXXX)
  # Variable used by the distcc client
  export INCLUDE_SERVER_PORT="$INCLUDE_SERVER_DIR/socket"

  mkdir -p "$OUTPUT"

  # TODO add a separator line to the stdout/stderr or rotate logs
  # Start the include server directly, avoiding the `pump` wrapper.
  # This allows more control, e.g. to chose the version of python
  # (not necessarily the one used to build )
  local cmd="PYTHONPATH='$PYTHONPATH:$include_server_install' \
    python '$include_server_install/include_server.py' \
      --port '$INCLUDE_SERVER_PORT' --pid_file '$pid_file' \
      $debug_args"
  if [ "$DEBUG_DISTCC" != true ]; then
    cmd="$cmd >'$OUTPUT/distcc-pump.stdout' 2>'$OUTPUT/distcc-pump.stderr'"
  fi
  eval $cmd

  # Variable used by "pump --shutdown" (see pump_shutdown)
  export INCLUDE_SERVER_PID=$(cat "$pid_file")
}


pump_shutdown() {
  # TODO add a separator line to the stdout/stderr or rotate logs
  pump --shutdown | grep -v '___Shutting down' || true
  # The $INCLUDE_SERVER_PORT socket and $INCLUDE_SERVER_DIR directory are removed by pump
  unset INCLUDE_SERVER_DIR INCLUDE_SERVER_PORT INCLUDE_SERVER_PID
}


setup_distcc_hosts() {
  # TODO setup_distcc_hosts is slow when outside CERN.
  # Consider doing port forwarding it a distcc wrapper.

  local distcc_env
  if ! distcc_env=$("$DIR/setup-distcc.py"); then
    return 1
  fi
  eval $distcc_env
}
```

<sub>993m 12s</sub>

### Reasoning

*I suspect a distcc remote host problem, since the remote compile is failing with exit 255. The compile script only turns off distcc inside the CMakeTmp directory, but CMake 3.30 uses CMakeScratch instead, so distcc is still active during configure and is likely failing there, possibly because of missing Kerberos setup.

I'm weighing whether to edit the shared compile.sh so it also skips distcc for CMakeScratch paths, or to just set useDistcc to false in the config, which is less invasive. Either way I need to confirm that distcc is actually the cause, so I'll test with it turned off first, running configure with a long timeout since the Detector compile can be slow.

The likely cause is that compile.sh disables distcc only in CMakeTmp, while CMake 3.30 runs the compiler test in CMakeScratch, so configure fails. I'll test that by turning distcc off in the config.*

<sub>1004m 57s</sub>

### Copilot

distcc is a tool that spreads C/C++ compilation across several machines. Each compile job runs on a remote server and sends the object file back, so a large build uses many more cores than your own machine has.

- **How it works.** The build runs the compiler through a `distcc` wrapper. It preprocesses locally, or uses the "pump" mode that your stack enables, and sends the work to remote hosts. The linking and the rest of the build stay on your machine.
- **Here.** The stack installs its own distcc fork from `gitlab.cern.ch/rmatev/distcc`, via `utils/install-distcc.sh`. It is used with ccache, which caches the results of earlier compiles. The remote hosts need Kerberos authentication, so `build-env` is called with `--require-kerberos-distcc`. I didn't check which hosts it uses. `useDistcc` in `utils/config.json` turns it on or off.
- **Why it's off now.** With it on, the CMake compiler test failed silently. As I said earlier, I only confirmed that turning it off fixes this, not why.
- **Cost of leaving it off.** The whole build runs on your local cores only, so it takes longer.

No, building the whole stack is not the only way. I haven't run any of these myself.

**1. A prebuilt Moore.** `lb-run` and `lb-dev` are on your PATH, and `/cvmfs/lhcb.cern.ch/lib/lhcb/MOORE` has released versions (up to `MOORE_v9r4`). `lb-run Moore/<version> gaudirun.py <options>` runs the existing `standalone_hlt2_seeding` options with no build. The catch is that released versions are Run 3 software. They contain `PrHybridSeeding`, but not necessarily the Run 5 geometry or your branch's code. I didn't find a prebuilt `lhcb-run5` nightly under `/cvmfs/lhcbdev.cern.ch`, though I only checked two paths.

**2. Build only the part you edit.** `lb-dev` can check out just Rec on top of a released Moore and build it in minutes. That works if your seeding change doesn't need Run 5 geometry.

**3. Build part of this stack.** `make Rec/PrAlgorithms` style targets (the Makefile has per-project targets). The dependencies must be built first, which is why Lbcom blocked you.

**4. Allen.** It has its own standalone executable for the GPU/CPU seeding. I did not check how it is run here.

**Input data:** every route needs a test file. Real MDF data covers the raw banks. MC checking needs a simulation file with MC links. I don't know which test files you have access to, so I can't say which route fits.

If you tell me which branch and detector version you want to test, I can say which one fits and what to run.

<sub>1050m 26s</sub>

### Copilot

No, not one you can run. There are Run 5 nightlies on CVMFS, but the Moore ones are not usable.

**What's there:** `/cvmfs/lhcbdev.cern.ch/nightlies/nightly/lhcb-run5/` holds builds 466–470. Build 458 is not deployed there.

**What's inside** (gcc15-opt, builds 466 and 470, same pattern):
- **Gaudi and Detector** have real install areas (9 and 8 entries).
- **LHCb, Lbcom, Rec, Allen and Moore** have empty install areas. The source trees are there, but no built libraries.

That matches the nightly status. LHCb already fails from build 459 on, so everything above it isn't built. A Moore from these nightlies can't run.

**What you could do instead**
- A released Moore from `/cvmfs/lhcb.cern.ch/lib/lhcb/MOORE` (up to `MOORE_v9r4`) with `lb-run`. It is Run 3 software and may not suit Run 5 geometry. I did not test it.
- Build the stack yourself. This is the route I was on: with Lbcom moved back to `ee3fbefa`, the build was passing Lbcom. I'll check where it has got to.

I checked only the gcc15-opt install areas and two build numbers.

<sub>1098m 22s</sub>

### Copilot

Yes. Dropping all of `PrMCTools` would break MC-based SciFi testing, because the whole module goes. It contains:
- `PrChecker.cpp`, which does the efficiency, ghost and clone checks for seeds
- `PrTrackAssociator`
- `PrLHCbID2MCParticle`
- `PrFTHitsChecker`
- `PrCheatedSciFiTracking`

The two files that fail are `FakeClusteringTV.cpp` and `DepositCreatorDetailed.cpp`. They are TV MC code that SciFi doesn't need, and `src/TVUPCheatedPR.cpp` and `src/TVUPTCheatedPR.cpp` may share the same TV `sensor` issue.

**Better option:** remove only those TV files from `Rec/Pr/PrMCTools/CMakeLists.txt`, at line 49 for `FakeClusteringTV.cpp` plus the `DepositCreatorDetailed` entry. Alternatively patch the three `sensor(int)` calls with `SensorID{n}`. Either way `PrChecker` and the SciFi checkers still build.

I haven't made either change yet. I can apply the CMake edit and rebuild if you want.

Only the TV files that fail to compile (`FakeClusteringTV.cpp`, `DepositCreatorDetailed.cpp`) need to go. `src/TVUPCheatedPR.cpp` and `src/TVUPTCheatedPR.cpp` may share the same TV `sensor` issue. You can instead patch the three `sensor(int)` calls with `SensorID{n}`. I have not made either change.

```bash

# 1. Branch from the current commit, so your work keeps the nightly-458 base

```

  ```bash
  git push -u fork xihu/fix-prmctools-tv-sensor
  ```
  Then open a merge request on GitLab.

```
@configurable
def tracking_efficiency(det, tracks, make_mc_track_info=make_track_info):
    det_options = ["TV", "FT", "MP", "UP", "MT", "VeloUP", "VeloUPFT"]
    category = {
        "TV": "Velo",
        "FT": "SeedFT",
        "MP": "SeedMP",
        "UP": "Upstream",
        "VeloUP": "Upstream",
        "VeloUPFT": "LongFTUP",
        "VeloUPMP": "LongMPUP",
        "MT": "Seed",
    }
    if det not in det_options:
        print(f"Error: unrecognised detector: {det}")
        return

    return check_tracking_efficiency(
        TrackType=det,
        InputTracks=tracks["Tracks"],
        LinksToTracks=tracks["TrackLinks"],
        LinksToLHCbIDs=tracks["ClusterLinks"],
        MCCategories=get_mc_categories(category[det]),
        HitTypesToCheck=get_hit_type_mask_u2(category[det]),  # remove
        MCPropertyInput=make_mc_track_info(),
    )

):

        trackType=Ttype,
        isFT=is_ft,

    )
```

```
@configurable
def get_ft_tracks(make_ft_hits=get_ft_hits):
    """Makes seed tracks with PrHybridSeeding [1]_.
    Args:
        make_ft_hits (DataHandle): maker of FT hits, defaults to `make_PrStoreSciFiHits_hits <RecoConf.hlt1_tracking.make_PrStoreSciFiHits_hits>`.
    Returns:
        A dict mapping v1 and v2 SciFi seeding tracks to ``'v1'`` and ``'v2'`` respectively.
    .. [1] https://cds.cern.ch/record/2027531/
    """
    ft_hits = get_ft_hits()
    scifi_tracks_pr = PrHybridSeeding(FTHitsLocation=ft_hits).OutputName
    scifi_tracks_v1 = fromPrSeedingTracksV1Tracks(
        InputTracksLocation=scifi_tracks_pr
    ).OutputTracksLocation
    return {"v1": scifi_tracks_v1, "Pr": scifi_tracks_pr}


@configurable
def get_pr_ft_tracks(make_ft_hits=get_ft_hits):
    """Makes seed tracks with PrHybridSeeding [1]_.
    Args:
        make_ft_hits (DataHandle): maker of FT hits, defaults to `make_PrStoreSciFiHits_hits <RecoConf.hlt1_tracking.make_PrStoreSciFiHits_hits>`.
    Returns:
        A dict mapping v1 and v2 SciFi seeding tracks to ``'v1'`` and ``'v2'`` respectively.
    .. [1] https://cds.cern.ch/record/2027531/
    """
    ft_hits = get_ft_hits()
    scifi_tracks_pr = PrHybridSeeding(FTHitsLocation=ft_hits).OutputName
    scifi_tracks_v1 = fromPrSeedingTracksV1Tracks(
        InputTracksLocation=scifi_tracks_pr
    ).OutputTracksLocation
    clusterlocation = make_FTRawBankDecoder_clusters()
    cluster2mcp = PrLHCbID2MCParticleFT(
        MCParticlesLocation=get_mc_particles(),
        FTLiteClustersLocation=clusterlocation,
        FTLiteClustersLinkLocation=ft_links_digits_mcparticles(),
    )
    track2mcp = make_links_tracks_mcparticles(
        InputTracks=scifi_tracks_v1, LinksToLHCbIDs=cluster2mcp
    )

    scifi_tracks_future = fromV1TrackFutureTrack(
        InputTracksName=scifi_tracks_v1
    ).OutputTracksName

    return {
        "v1": scifi_tracks_v1,
        "Pr": scifi_tracks_pr,
        "Tracks": scifi_tracks_future,
        "TrackLinks": track2mcp,
        "ClusterLinks": cluster2mcp,
        "Clusters": clusterlocation,
    }
```

```
I ran the Run 5 SciFi seeding test myself, and it finished cleanly (rc=0, 20 events), so no input file was needed from you. I used the Run 5 simulated sample `upgrade2_minbias_1p0e34_Jan2026`, a DIGI file with MC truth, from CVMFS (geometry `run5/proto-v00.03`, conditions `sim11/run5-ideal`).

**Results (`FTTrackChecker`, `PrHybridSeeding`, 20 events)**
- Ghost rate: 13.6% (4723 tracks, 643 ghosts), 11.1% as an event average.
- Long tracks: 89.5% efficient for the FT-reconstructible ones (2388 of 2668), purity 99.4%.
- Long tracks above 5 GeV: 97.0% efficient (1132 of 1167), purity 99.4%.
- Clones: 0%.

**Files**
- `run5_ft_seeding_test.py` is the new options file. Run it with `cd run5_test && ../Moore/run gaudirun.py ../run5_ft_seeding_test.py`. The log is `run5_test/log.txt`, plus `run5_seeding_histos.root` and `run5_seeding_tuple.root`.
- The existing `standalone_hlt2_seeding` example doesn't run on Run 5, because it pulls in Hlt2 physics lines that don't work with Moore's Run 5 config. The new script uses `get_pr_ft_tracks` and `tracking_efficiency("FT", ...)` instead.

**Changes**
- Rec: the three `DeTV::sensor(...)` calls in `PrMCTools` now use `TVChannelID::SensorID(...)` (commit `914256b466` on `xihu/fix-prmctools-tv-sensor`, not pushed). This replaces the earlier approach of removing the two TV files, because Moore's Run 5 reconstruction imports those algorithms.
- Detector: I added a new geometry copy, `compact/run5/proto-v00.03-picocalfix`, using PicoCal `proto-run5-v01.00`. The original PicoCal version lacks a constant the Detector PicoCal builder needs, and PicoCal doesn't affect SciFi. The original geometry is untouched.
```

<sub>1144m 51s</sub>

### ✓ Task Complete

I ran the Run 5 SciFi seeding test myself, and it finished cleanly (rc=0, 20 events), so no input file was needed from you. I used the Run 5 simulated sample `upgrade2_minbias_1p0e34_Jan2026`, a DIGI file with MC truth, from CVMFS (geometry `run5/proto-v00.03`, conditions `sim11/run5-ideal`).

**Results (`FTTrackChecker`, `PrHybridSeeding`, 20 events)**
- Ghost rate: 13.6% (4723 tracks, 643 ghosts), 11.1% as an event average.
- Long tracks: 89.5% efficient for the FT-reconstructible ones (2388 of 2668), purity 99.4%.
- Long tracks above 5 GeV: 97.0% efficient (1132 of 1167), purity 99.4%.
- Clones: 0%.

**Files**
- `run5_ft_seeding_test.py` is the new options file. Run it with `cd run5_test && ../Moore/run gaudirun.py ../run5_ft_seeding_test.py`. The log is `run5_test/log.txt`, plus `run5_seeding_histos.root` and `run5_seeding_tuple.root`.
- The existing `standalone_hlt2_seeding` example doesn't run on Run 5, because it pulls in Hlt2 physics lines that don't work with Moore's Run 5 config. The new script uses `get_pr_ft_tracks` and `tracking_efficiency("FT", ...)` instead.

**Changes**
- Rec: the three `DeTV::sensor(...)` calls in `PrMCTools` now use `TVChannelID::SensorID(...)` (commit `914256b466` on `xihu/fix-prmctools-tv-sensor`, not pushed). This replaces the earlier approach of removing the two TV files, because Moore's Run 5 reconstruction imports those algorithms.
- Detector: I added a new geometry copy, `compact/run5/proto-v00.03-picocalfix`, using PicoCal `proto-run5-v01.00`. The original PicoCal version lacks a constant the Detector PicoCal builder needs, and PicoCal doesn't affect SciFi. The original geometry is untouched.

The guide walks through:
1. **Setup:** the `lb-stack-setup` one-liner, the kerberos and GitLab ssh prerequisites, and copying `scifi_run5_work/` into the new stack.
2. **Configuration:** answer `lhcb-run5` at the prompt, then run `utils/config.py useDistcc false`.
3. **Checkout:** run the checkout script for nightly `lhcb-run5/458`, then run `make purge` and `make Moore` themselves.
4. **Fixes:** move Lbcom to `ee3fbefa` and apply the Rec patch. Nightly 458 doesn't build without them.
5. **Build:** `make Moore`, with what success looks like and how to rebuild or debug a single project.
6. **Geometry:** the PicoCal geometry copy, with the exact commands.
7. **Test:** run `run5_ft_seeding_test.py` on the CVMFS sample, with a table of our results to compare against.
8. **Known issues:** the Run 3 standalone example, the disabled `PhoenixAlgs`, and the failures in nightly 458.

I corrected the README, which wrongly said the checkout script runs `make purge && make Moore`.

```
class PrTrackFitterYZ final {
  static constexpr size_t N_MAX_HITS   = LHCb::Detector::FT::nUVLayersTotal;
  static constexpr float  ZREF         = LHCb::Pr::Hybrid::zReference;
  static constexpr int    N_FIT_PARAMS = 2;

  using TrackType    = const LHCb::Pr::Hybrid::SeedTrackX;
  using TrackTypeRef = TrackType&;
  using MatrixType   = LHCb::LinAlg::MatSym<float, N_FIT_PARAMS>;
  using VectorType   = LHCb::LinAlg::Vec<float, N_FIT_PARAMS>;
  using PrSciFiHits  = LHCb::Pr::FT::Hits;

public:
  PrTrackFitterYZ()                                    = delete;
  PrTrackFitterYZ( const PrTrackFitterYZ& )            = delete;
  PrTrackFitterYZ( PrTrackFitterYZ&& )                 = delete;
  PrTrackFitterYZ& operator=( const PrTrackFitterYZ& ) = delete;
  PrTrackFitterYZ& operator=( PrTrackFitterYZ&& )      = delete;

  PrTrackFitterYZ( TrackType& track ) : m_track( track ) {}

  float       chi2PerDoF() const noexcept { return m_chi2PerDoF; }
  const auto& chi2Hits() const noexcept { return m_chi2Hits; }
  auto&       chi2Hits() noexcept { return m_chi2Hits; }
  float       ay() const noexcept { return m_ay; }
  float       by() const noexcept { return m_by; }

  template <typename HitIteratorType>
  bool fit( const PrSciFiHits& sciFiHits, HitIteratorType itBeg, HitIteratorType itEnd ) noexcept {
    VectorType rhs; // right-hand-side of the linear system (function of the x positions)
    MatrixType mat; // matrix of the linear system

    initialize_linear_system( sciFiHits, itBeg, itEnd, mat, rhs );

    float det = mat( 0, 0 ) * mat( 1, 1 ) - mat( 0, 1 ) * mat( 1, 0 );
    if ( LHCb::essentiallyZero( det ) ) return false;

    const float invDet = 1.f / det;
    m_ay               = ( rhs( 0 ) * mat( 1, 1 ) - mat( 0, 1 ) * rhs( 1 ) ) * invDet;
    m_by               = ( mat( 0, 0 ) * rhs( 1 ) - rhs( 0 ) * mat( 1, 0 ) ) * invDet;

    calculate_chi2( sciFiHits, itBeg, itEnd );

    return true;
  }

private:
  template <typename HitIteratorType>
  void calculate_chi2( const PrSciFiHits& sciFiHits, HitIteratorType itBeg, HitIteratorType itEnd ) noexcept {
    m_chi2PerDoF = 0.f;
    for ( auto [iterH, iterChi2] = std::tuple{ itBeg, m_chi2Hits.begin() }; itEnd != iterH; ++iterH, ++iterChi2 ) {
      *iterChi2 = chi2hit( sciFiHits, **iterH );
      m_chi2PerDoF += *iterChi2;
    }
    m_chi2PerDoF /= ( itEnd - itBeg - N_FIT_PARAMS );
  }
```

<sub>1202m 47s</sub>

### Copilot

A t‑z fit with two free parameters is feasible only if you constrain it with physics. These are the main points.

**Hit time model**

t_i = t0 + L_i/(βc) + t_prop(y_i) + noise

- **t0** is the collision time at the track origin. It is shared by all tracks from the same vertex.
- **L_i** is the path length from the origin to the hit. It is about z_i·√(1+tx²+ty²), and the x‑z and y‑z fits already give tx and ty. It is not purely linear in z, but it is close.
- **t_prop(y_i)** is the signal propagation along the fibre to the SiPM. The distance is |y_i − y_readout|, and the delay is roughly 5–6 ns/m, so it can reach about 10 ns for half-length fibres. It must be subtracted using the y of the hit, which comes from the y‑z fit. Without it, the t‑z relation is dominated by a y-dependent offset.
- **Hit time and resolution.** I haven't checked whether Run 5 SciFi hits carry a time or what resolution they have. Everything below depends on that.

**Choosing the two extra parameters**

1. **(t0, 1/β) both free.** The lever arm is about 1.8 m in z, which is about 6 ns of flight time. With ~100 ps hit resolution, the slope is determined to about 1–2%. That is poor for β≈0.99 pions, and it is only useful for slow protons or kaons. The two parameters are also strongly correlated.
2. **t0 free, slope fixed to 1/c (recommended).** This is a one-parameter fit that is stable, and I'd use it as the baseline. A slow-particle hypothesis can be added later with a momentum-dependent β, since the seed already has a momentum estimate from cx.
3. **t0 constrained by the PV.** t0 + z_origin/c must be consistent with a bunch-crossing time (σ ≈ 180 ps) and with the 4D Velo vertex time. This is the strongest use of timing at high pile-up, because it separates hits and tracks from different collisions.

**Where to use it in the code**

- **Hit finding and ghost rejection.** Cut on the residual of t_i − L_i/c − t_prop against a common t0, before or alongside the x‑z candidate chi2.
- **Final fit.** Add a time term to `PrTrackFitterXYZ.h`, giving a 6‑parameter fit (ax, bx, cx, ay, by, t0). The time chi2 is added to the spatial chi2.

Do you want me to check the FT hit data first to see whether a time field exists and what its resolution is? If it does, I'd prototype option 2 as a hit-time consistency cut in `PrHybridSeeding` and measure the effect on ghosts and efficiency on the 1.5e34 sample.

<sub>1203m 57s</sub>

### Copilot

A 7-parameter fit (at, bt) is possible. I preferred 6 because the slope bt is physically close to fixed, and fitting it costs more than it gains.

**Why the slope is nearly fixed**
- bt ≈ 1/(βc) × √(1+tx²+ty²).
- tx and ty already come from the x‑z and y‑z fits. For β ≈ 1 the slope is therefore known and not free.
- The only unknown part of the slope is β, and it depends on the mass and momentum of the particle.

**Why fitting bt hurts**
- **Weak lever arm.** SciFi spans about 1.8 m in z, which is about 6 ns of flight time. With ~100 ps hit resolution, bt is determined at roughly the 1–2% level. A pion at 1 GeV has β ≈ 0.99, so its slope differs from 1/c by about 1%. The fit cannot separate it from noise.
- **Strong correlation.** at and bt are highly correlated because the hits sit far from z = 0. That inflates the variance of t0, and t0 is the parameter that rejects pile-up.
- **Fewer constraints for ghost rejection.** A free slope absorbs some of the time inconsistency that a ghost would otherwise show. Fixing it makes the time test sharper.
- **Few hits.** A seed has at most 12 hits, and they are already used for 5 spatial parameters.

**When 7 parameters make sense**
- Slow particles, such as protons and low-momentum kaons, where β is clearly below 1.
- A much better time resolution than 100 ps, for example about 30 ps.
- Particle identification, where β is the quantity you want to measure.

**A middle option**
Use bt = 1/(βc) with β computed from the momentum estimate (from cx) and a mass hypothesis. This gives the 6‑parameter fit a slope that is correct for slow particles without making it a free parameter. If the data later show a significant β effect, you can promote it to a free parameter and compare the 6‑ and 7‑parameter fits on the same sample.

I haven't checked whether the Run 5 hits carry timing, so the resolution figures above are assumed.

The reference plane, such as the middle of the SciFi, would decouple at from bt, and t0 would only come back after matching to the vertex.

I'm noting that the at intercept carries a spread of about 170 ps from the z0 spread of roughly 50 mm, which is comparable to the bunch time spread and fits a 4D primary vertex. <sub>1205m 3s</sub>

### Copilot

**Relation between (at, bt) and t0**

Write the hit time as a straight line in z:

t_i = at + bt·z_i

For a track from origin (x0, y0, z0) at time t0, with the SciFi path approximated as straight:

- bt = k/(βc), where k = √(1+tx²+ty²), so bt is the slope of t against z.
- at = t0 − bt·z0, which is the line extrapolated to z = 0.
- Going the other way, t0 = at + bt·z0.

The hit times must first be corrected for fibre propagation, using y from the y‑z fit. After that correction, t_i is the time of flight plus t0. The straight-path form is an approximation, because the track bends in the magnet. L_i should really be the integrated path length with a curvature correction.

**What is degenerate**

1. **t0 and z0.** The SciFi seed measures only at = t0 − bt·z0. A track from a vertex that is later by Δt is indistinguishable from one whose origin is shifted by Δz0 = cΔt. The seed alone cannot give t0. You need z0 from the matched Velo track or the PV. The PV z spread (σ ≈ 50 mm, about 170 ps) is as large as the bunch-time spread, so without z0 the measured at is smeared by that amount.
2. **at and bt.** Hits sit at z ≈ 7.7–9.4 m, far from z = 0, so the two are almost perfectly anticorrelated. Fitting the line as t = a' + bt·(z − z_ref), with z_ref near the SciFi centre, removes most of this correlation. The 6‑ and 7‑parameter fits are equivalent in information but numerically better conditioned this way.
3. **β, mass and momentum.** bt gives β only. That does not separate p from m unless the curvature (cx) supplies p.
4. **k and β.** If tx and ty are not fixed from the spatial fit, a change in k looks like a change in β. In the sequential fit they are fixed, so the problem is only conceptual there.
5. **Offsets.** A per-module or per-channel time offset (calibration or propagation constant) cannot be told apart from at. These offsets must be calibrated beforehand.

For seeding, the quantity to fit and cut on is at (or the time at z_ref). t0 only appears once the seed is matched to a vertex.

<sub>1210m 19s</sub>

### Copilot

That count doesn't hold, and I should tighten my earlier "few hits" argument too.

**Measurements per hit**
- A SciFi hit is a 1D measurement. Each fibre layer measures one coordinate, the position across the fibres. For x layers that is x. For the stereo layers (±5°) it is x cosθ + y sinθ.
- z is not measured, since it is the known layer position. y is not measured by an x layer and only enters weakly through the stereo layers.
- So 12 hits give 12 measurements, not 36. The spatial fit has 12 measurements and 5 parameters, which leaves 7 degrees of freedom.

**With time**
- If every hit has a time, that adds 12 more measurements, so 24 in total, not 48.
- A 6‑parameter fit (ax, bx, cx, ay, by, at) leaves 18 degrees of freedom. A 7‑parameter fit leaves 17.
- Time therefore more than doubles the number of constraints for the same hit set, and it is useful for ghost rejection.

**What "few hits" should have meant**
The degrees of freedom are not the issue. The problem is the time-fit precision:
- The time lever arm is small: about 6 ns of flight time across the SciFi z range.
- The resolution per hit is unknown to me, probably around 100 ps.
- The at–bt correlation is strong.

With 12 time measurements, σ(slope) improves as ~1/√N, but that only reaches the 1–2% level I estimated. This is still comparable to the β deviation of fast particles, so the slope is poorly determined.

Two caveats on the 12 hits:
- Not every seed has all 12 layers. The minimum is typically 9–10 hits, so the dof are fewer.
- Per-hit times are not independent. They share the fibre-propagation correction through y, and the correction's error propagates from the y‑z fit.

Fitting the slope is therefore feasible once the resolution is known. If the hit time resolution is about 30 ps or better, the 7‑parameter fit becomes worth it. That is why I suggest comparing the two fits on the same sample.

<sub>1212m 50s</sub>

### Copilot

Yes, you're right. The concern is the same for both fits, and it does not favour 6 parameters over 7.

**Degrees of freedom with fewer layers**

Take a seed with N hits, each with a space and a time measurement:

| Fit | Measurements | Parameters | dof |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6‑parameter | 2N | 6 | 2N − 6 |
| 7‑parameter | 2N | 7 | 2N − 7 |

For N = 9, that is 12 dof with 6 parameters and 11 with 7. Both are comfortable, so a seed with fewer than 12 layers does not rule out the 7‑parameter fit.

**Where the real difference lies**

- The fewer hits there are, the shorter the z lever arm, and the worse the at–bt correlation and the σ(bt) become. That affects both fits, but the 7‑parameter fit suffers more, because it must determine bt and the 6‑parameter fit does not.
- With 6 parameters, bt is fixed and only at is fitted. A missing layer barely changes σ(at).
- With 7 parameters, a missing layer at the ends of the z range cuts the lever arm sharply. The slope uncertainty can then grow beyond the point where the slope carries any information, and the fit adds noise.

**What I'd do**

- Make the choice per seed: fit 7 parameters only when N is large enough and the z span is wide enough that σ(bt) is below the β effect you want to see. Otherwise fall back to the 6‑parameter fit with a fixed slope. This is the same kind of fallback the spatial fit already uses for short candidates.
- Whichever fit you use, apply the same minimum-hit requirement as the spatial seed. Currently that is roughly 9–10 hits.

I haven't checked this against the code or measured σ(bt) on the sample. The suggestion follows from the lever-arm argument, so the threshold should be set from data.

```
      tmp[i]         = inv * inv;
    }
    return tmp;
  }();
```

### Copilot

Yes for position, no for time. I checked the position errors in the code. For time I only have assumptions.

**Position uncertainty (found in the code)**

In `Rec/Pr/PrAlgorithms/src/PrStoreSciFiHits.cpp` (line 41), the hit weight is 1/σ², with σ set by the cluster size (`pseudoSize`):

| pseudoSize | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| σ (mm) | 0.05 | 0.08 | 0.11 | 0.14 | 0.17 | 0.20 | 0.23 | 0.26 | 0.29 |

(The file has a `TODO: get this from a tool?`, so these are hard-coded.) A few consequences:
- **Only one position coordinate is measured.** This is x for the x layers and the stereo-projected coordinate for the U/V layers. There is no separate y uncertainty and no separate z uncertainty (z is fixed by the layer).
- **y is inferred.** The y precision comes from the stereo projection: σ_y ≈ σ_x / tan(5°), roughly 11 times worse than σ_x, before fitting.
- **Units.** I read the numbers as mm from the style of the code, but I did not check the unit explicitly.

**Timing uncertainty (not in the code)**

I found no time field or time resolution in the seeding or in the hit creator. Here is what I am assuming:
- The Run 5 SciFi / Mighty Tracker time resolution is not something I can quote reliably. My earlier ~100 ps was a placeholder, not a measured value.
- A plausible budget would combine the intrinsic SiPM and electronics resolution, the fibre-propagation spread and the clock/calibration jitter. The propagation term is about 5–6 ns/m of fibre, so an uncertainty in y of 10 cm adds roughly 0.5–0.6 ns. That is likely the dominant term unless y is known to better than a few mm.

This matters for the design: the time term is weighted properly only if y is known well. Since σ_y from the stereo layers is poor, the propagation correction can dominate the time error. The y‑z fit therefore needs to be good before the time fit.

To pin it down, I'd look for the time resolution in the Run 5 TDR or simulation configuration, or in the DIGI sample's cluster contents. I can search the `FTLiteCluster` definition and the MC DIGI sample next if you want.

<sub>1217m 11s</sub>

### User

You said that to fix bt. To fix to what value?

---

<sub>1217m 19s</sub>

### Copilot

Fix it to the speed-of-light value for the track's own direction, with a small refinement for the path length.

**The value**

bt = k/c, where k = √(1+tx²+ty²) and c = 299.792 mm/ns, so 1/c ≈ 3.3356 ps/mm.

- For a nearly forward track (tx, ty ≈ 0), bt ≈ 3.34 ns/m. Across the 1.8 m SciFi lever arm that is about 6 ns.
- tx and ty are the track slopes from the x‑z and y‑z fits. They differ per seed, which is why bt is fixed per seed rather than globally.
- Large-angle tracks have k noticeably above 1. For tx ≈ 0.3, k ≈ 1.04, a 4% change in slope, or about 0.25 ns over the lever arm. That is far larger than the time resolution, so k must be included.

**Two refinements, with my caveats**

1. **Curvature.** The track bends in the magnet, so the SciFi-local slopes are not the slopes of the whole path from the origin. A more accurate L uses the integrated path length, for example from the momentum estimate and the field. A first version could ignore this and compare the residual distribution to see whether it matters. I haven't quantified how large the bending error is.
2. **β \< 1.** Fixing 1/β = 1 is wrong for slow particles. For a proton at 2 GeV/c, β ≈ 0.90, so the slope is about 11% too small, which is about 0.7 ns over the lever arm. Those tracks will show a systematic time residual. A better choice, once the momentum is available from cx, is 1/β = √(1 + m²/p²) with a mass assumption, such as the pion mass as default. Protons then show up as outliers, and the seed can be refit with a proton mass if you want to recover them.

**Practical recommendation**

Start with bt = k/c using the pion mass, measure the time residuals on MC truth tracks separated by particle type, and only then decide whether a free slope or a mass-dependent slope is needed. That decision needs data, and I have not yet run it.

<sub>1218m 8s</sub>

### User

you mean, fit (x,y) vs z first, to get tx and ty. Right?

---

<sub>1218m 13s</sub>

### Copilot

Yes. The time fit comes after the spatial fit, and it uses the spatial fit's results.

**Order**

1. **x‑z fit:** ax, bx, cx. This gives tx(z) = bx + 2·cx·dz plus the small `dRatio` correction.
2. **y‑z fit:** ay, by, with ty = by.
3. **Optional refit of all five parameters (XYZ).** This improves tx, ty and y.
4. **Time correction and fit:**
   - From the final spatial parameters, get y_i at each hit and compute the propagation delay t_prop(y_i).
   - Compute k = √(1+tx²+ty²) and the path length L_i.
   - Compute the residual r_i = t_i − t_prop(y_i) − L_i/c, which should be flat in z if the seed is real.
   - Fit one parameter, at (equivalently the weighted mean of r_i), and use the χ² of the residuals as the time test.

**Two caveats**

- **Evaluation point.** tx changes along the track because the x‑z fit is a parabola. For L_i, use the local slope or integrate the path between layers, not one global tx.
- **Possible iteration.** The time information could in principle improve the spatial fit by rejecting wrong hits, and that in turn would improve tx, ty and y. I would not iterate at first. Do the sequential fit, then check how large the time-fit errors are from imperfect tx, ty and y before deciding whether iteration is worth it.

That keeps the existing spatial fit unchanged and adds the time step afterwards.

It looks like the approach LHCb uses for its Velo 4D tracking, and it's valid, though it may not really differ from my own seven-parameter model with the bt constraint. I'm also noting that a linear t(z) is only approximate, since the path length depends on the slopes tx and ty as they vary.

I'm checking the time term more carefully: the measured time depends on the transverse position y through the propagation time, so t and y are coupled. Because that propagation term is linear in the y-parameters, the joint fit stays linear, though the time measurement adds little information on y itself.

I'm now seeing that the time slope mixes bt with the y-slope, so they're only partly separable, though stereo pins y well enough that the sequential fit works in practice. I agree the seven-parameter model is the natural one and my earlier six was just a choice. I'd recommend fitting seven parameters with a Gaussian prior on bt around k/c, its width set by the spread in β.*

<sub>1219m 3s</sub>

### Copilot

It is a natural formulation, and I think it is a good one. It mirrors the way the Velo 4D Kalman code carries `t` as a state component alongside x and y. My 6‑parameter version is just the 7‑parameter fit with bt frozen, so the two are not in conflict.

**The 7‑parameter model**
- x(z): ax, bx, cx.
- y(z): ay, by.
- t(z): at, bt.

**Caveats that apply to this formulation**

1. **The time measurement also depends on y.** The measured hit time includes the fibre propagation delay, which is roughly (Y_readout − y_i)/v_fibre, where v is the signal speed in the fibre. Substituting y_i = ay + by·z_i gives a delay that is linear in ay and by. So the time residuals are not independent of the y‑z parameters. The system stays linear, but it is a joint fit, not three separate ones. The effective time slope is then bt − by/v (up to a sign), so bt and by partly mix. In practice the stereo layers pin y much better than the timing does (σ_y of order 1 mm against the ~10 mm that 100 ps corresponds to in the fibre), so this mixing is small. It becomes a real issue only if the y fit is poor.
2. **bt is not an independent quantity physically.** It equals k/(βc), with k = √(1+tx²+ty²), so it is tied to bx and by. Treating it as free discards that constraint. A good compromise is a Gaussian prior on bt, centred on k/c with a width that reflects the β spread. This gives a fit that is "free" in principle, stays stable when the time lever arm is weak, and still recovers slow particles. A prior width of zero reproduces my 6‑parameter fit, and an infinite width gives your 7‑parameter fit.
3. **t(z) is only approximately linear.** Path length is not exactly proportional to z because of the parabola and the magnet bend, so the model has a small systematic curvature. A linear t(z) will leave a residual trend that grows with the track bending, which I have not quantified.
4. **at carries the t0 and z0 degeneracy** as discussed. The fit gives at, not t0.

So I'd implement the 7‑parameter joint fit with the prior on bt, and compare it on MC against bt fixed (6 parameters) and bt fully free. I'd do this in the same step I mentioned before, once the hit time field and resolution are confirmed. Without that, the prior width and the weights in the time part of the χ² cannot be set.

<sub>1232m 30s</sub>

### User

summarize the fitting procedure of the original scheme and the two different schemes (6 and 7 parameters)

---

<sub>1232m 40s</sub>

### Copilot

**Original scheme (5 parameters, space only)**

1. **x‑z fit:** parabola with a small cubic correction (`dRatio`): ax, bx, cx. It uses the x-layer hits to find candidates.
2. **y‑z fit:** line, ay and by, fitted on the stereo U/V hits given the x‑z candidate.
3. **XYZ refit:** all five parameters (ax, bx, cx, ay, by) refitted together.
- Measurements: one position per hit (12 hits give 12 measurements, 7 dof). Hit weight is 1/σ² with σ from the cluster size (0.05–0.29 mm).
- Time: not used.

**Scheme A: 6 parameters (bt fixed)**

1. Do steps 1–3 above, unchanged.
2. From the final parameters, compute at each hit: the local slopes tx, ty, k = √(1+tx²+ty²), y_i, the path length L_i and the fibre delay t_prop(y_i).
3. Form the residuals r_i = t_i − t_prop(y_i) − L_i/c.
4. Fit one parameter, at, as the weighted mean of r_i. Use the time χ² as a consistency test or ghost cut.
- Slope: fixed to k/c, with optionally 1/β from a mass hypothesis and the momentum from cx.
- Measurements: 2N, parameters 6, so 2N − 6 dof.
- Pros: stable, spatial fit untouched, sharpest ghost rejection.
- Cons: biased for slow particles, and any error in tx, ty or y feeds into the time test without being fitted.

**Scheme B: 7 parameters (joint (x, y, t) vs z)**

1. Fit x(z) with ax, bx, cx, y(z) with ay, by, and t(z) with at, bt in one linear system.
2. Include the fibre delay (Y_readout − y_i)/v as a term linear in ay and by, so the y and t fits are coupled.
3. Optionally add a Gaussian prior on bt around k/c. The width sets where you sit between schemes: width 0 gives scheme A, infinite width gives a completely free slope.
- Measurements: 2N, parameters 7, so 2N − 7 dof.
- Pros: slow particles are handled naturally, the time constraint can feed back into the spatial fit, and the model is symmetric across x, y and t.
- Cons: at and bt are strongly correlated unless z is centred on a reference point. The slope is poorly determined with a short lever arm or few layers. It is more sensitive to the y‑z fit.

**Common points to both**

- Only at (the time extrapolated to z = 0) is measured. t0 needs the origin z0 from the Velo track or the PV.
- Hit time and resolution are not confirmed in the code. The weights in the time part of the χ² cannot be set until they are.
- Both fits assume the path is straight apart from a per-hit slope. Curvature from the magnet is neglected.
- Proposed comparison on MC: original, 6, 7 with prior, and 7 free, measured by efficiency, ghost rate, and the time residual width for pions against protons.

<sub>1233m 10s</sub>

### Reasoning

*I'm recalling that SciFi has three stations with four layers each, in an x-u-v-x arrangement, which gives six x layers and three each of the stereo U and V layers. There are no pure y layers, so y isn't measured directly. The seed uses T1 through T3, and I'm confident of this from what I know.*

---

<sub>1233m 10s</sub>

### Copilot

Out of 12 hits, 6 are x, 6 are stereo and none are y.

SciFi has 3 stations, each with 4 layers in the order x‑u‑v‑x:

- **x layers:** 6 (2 per station). Fibres are vertical, so they measure x.
- **Stereo layers:** 6, split into 3 U (+5°) and 3 V (−5°). They measure x cosθ + y sinθ.
- **y layers:** 0. No layer measures y directly.

So y comes only from the difference between the stereo and x measurements. That is why σ_y is about 1/tan 5° ≈ 11 times worse than σ_x, as I said earlier. It is also why the y‑z fit is done on the stereo hits given the x‑z candidate.

This affects how many constraints each fit really has. The x‑z fit has 6 measurements for 3 parameters. The y‑z fit has 6 stereo measurements for 2 parameters, and these are also used for the 5‑parameter XYZ refit.

I also changed the residual in step 3 to r_i = t_i − τ_i − S(z_i)/(βc), which is the data minus this model at at = 0.
